The derivative of x² at x = 5.6 is **11.2**.  Wolfram|Alpha's result panel shows "Result: 11.2", with the underlying derivative as d/dx(x²) = 2x, so 2 × 5.6 = 11.2. I ran the query at https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=derivative+of+x%5E2+when+x%3D5.6.

3^71 = 7.5094665… × 10^33, which rounds to **7.5095 × 10^33** at five significant figures.  Wolfram|Alpha returned the full value 7509466514979724803946715958257547 (34 digits) and the scientific notation 7.509466514979724803946715958257547 × 10^33. The sixth significant digit is 6, so the fifth digit rounds up from 7.5094 to 7.5095. My own logarithm estimate gave the same result.

The definite integral of 3e^(2x) from x=0 to x=5 is **3/2 (e^10 − 1) ≈ 33038.2**.  I ran the query on wolframalpha.com. The result panel shows the definite integral as "integral_0^5 3 e^(2x) dx = 3/2 (e^10 − 1) ≈ 33038." The indefinite antiderivative it lists is (3e^(2x))/2 + constant.

**9,675 days** between February 12, 2024 and August 9, 2050.  I searched on wolframalpha.com with "days between February 12, 2024 and August 9, 2050". The result panel shows "Result: 9675 days", with the input read as Monday, February 12, 2024 to Tuesday, August 9, 2050. The same page gives a time span of 26 years 5 months 28 days.  I also checked this by hand: 26 years contain 7 leap days (2024, 2028, …, 2048), so 26 × 365 + 7 = 9,497 days to February 12, 2050. From February 12 to August 9, 2050 is 178 days, giving 9,675.

The area of a regular hexagon with a 7 cm side is **(147√3)/2 cm² ≈ 127.306 cm²**.  I got this from WolframAlpha. I searched "area of a regular hexagon with side length 7 cm", and its result panel shows that exact form and the decimal approximation. The same panel gives the equivalent 0.01273 m² and 0.137 ft².

**Converges.** Wolfram|Alpha returned a closed form for the sum, which is finite. Its "Alternate form" is 1/3·(−1 + γ − ψ-terms), where γ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant and the ψ-terms are polygamma values. The page's alt text showed no numerical value, so I haven't read one off it.  The convergence doesn't depend on Wolfram|Alpha. Since 1/(n³+1) ~ 1/n³ as n → ∞, the limit comparison test with Σ 1/n³ (a p-series with p = 3 > 1) gives a finite nonzero limit, so the series converges.
